opus-5.5.text:
I think video games are, in a way, the perfect sandbox for developing general intelligence, for a few reasons.

First, they're environments designed by humans, for humans. Game designers spend enormous effort making games challenging, interesting, and diverse. That gives us a rich set of problems that require perception, planning, memory, long-term credit assignment, and sometimes even social reasoning. And they're designed to be hard for people, so they naturally probe the kinds of capabilities we care about.

Second, they give you a clean, well-defined signal. There's a score, or you win or lose. In reinforcement learning, you need a reward, and in the real world defining that reward is often the hardest part. Games hand it to you, so you can focus on the learning algorithm itself.

Third, and practically very important, they're fast and cheap to simulate. You can run millions of episodes in parallel and generate as much experience as your algorithm needs. You can't do that with a robot in the real world. That let us iterate quickly on ideas. With DQN on Atari, for example, a single algorithm with the same hyperparameters learned to play dozens of very different games from raw pixels. That generality was the point: we weren't building a Breakout agent, we were testing whether one learning system could adapt to many different worlds.

And games give you a natural curriculum of difficulty. You go from Atari to Go, which has an enormous search space and requires intuition and planning, to StarCraft or Dota, with partial observability, long time horizons, and multiple agents. Each step stresses a different part of intelligence.

Of course, games aren't the end goal. The real test is whether the techniques transfer beyond them. And we've seen that happen: ideas from AlphaGo and AlphaZero, combining learned models with search, went into MuZero, and those ideas now show up in video compression, chip design, and increasingly in how we think about reasoning and planning in large language models. So games were never about games. They were a controlled laboratory for building the core ingredients of general intelligence.

r002.rationale: It describes adapting across many games, but does not present Shane Legg’s conception of AGI as learning to complete any task.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think video games are useful for a few reasons, and they're mostly practical rather than philosophical.

The first is that games give you a clean, well-defined objective. You have a score, you have a win condition, and that means you can measure progress precisely. When we started working on Atari games at DeepMind, the appeal was that we could take one algorithm, one network architecture, and ask it to learn fifty or so very different games directly from pixels, with the same hyperparameters. If it could do that, you had some evidence of generality. You weren't hand-engineering a solution for each problem.

The second is that games are simulators, so you can generate essentially unlimited experience. Reinforcement learning is hungry for data, and in the real world collecting experience is slow, expensive, and sometimes dangerous. In a game you can run millions of episodes, reset whenever you like, and iterate on ideas quickly. That speed of iteration matters enormously for research.

The third is that games span a whole spectrum of difficulty. Atari tests perception and short-horizon control. Go tests long-horizon planning and intuition over an enormous search space. StarCraft adds partial observability, real-time decisions, and multi-agent dynamics. So you have a ladder of challenges, and each rung forces you to develop new ideas rather than just scale up the old ones.

And finally, there's a human benchmark. People have played these games for decades, so when a system reaches or exceeds expert human level, that's a meaningful, interpretable milestone. It's not the end goal, of course. The real test is whether the methods transfer to problems outside games, and that's what we've been pushing toward. But as a proving ground, games have been remarkably productive.

r002.rationale: It does not present Shane Legg’s conception of AGI as a system capable of learning to complete any task.

r003.rationale: It describes games as simulators where experience can be generated, episodes reset, and systems tested across challenges of varying difficulty.

astra-6.text:
Video games give us a way to study intelligence in environments where we can run experiments quickly and measure progress. They require an agent to look at what’s happening, make decisions, and deal with the consequences of those decisions over time. Often, you have to plan quite far ahead rather than just choose the action that gives you an immediate reward.

What’s particularly interesting is whether the same learning algorithm can learn to play many different games without us building a separate solution for each one. That gets at the question of generality: can the system acquire the skills it needs through experience?

Of course, being good at games doesn’t by itself mean you have artificial general intelligence. But games provide a controlled setting in which to develop and test some of the capabilities we think will matter.

r002.rationale: The response discusses learning across different games, but does not present Shane Legg’s conception of AGI as learning to complete any task.

r003.rationale: It describes games as a controlled setting for developing and testing capabilities relevant to general intelligence.

sol-6.1.text:
Video games give us a way to study intelligence in environments where an agent has to act, rather than simply produce an answer. It has to observe what’s happening, make decisions, and deal with the consequences. Often it needs to plan many steps ahead, and the reward for a good decision may come much later.

They’re also useful experimentally. We can run many games, measure progress, and vary the challenges. You can ask whether an agent is learning a strategy that generalizes or just becoming very good at one particular situation.

Of course, being good at a game doesn’t by itself mean you have general intelligence. But games give us a controlled setting for developing and testing some of the capabilities we think general intelligence will require: learning, planning, exploration, and adapting to new situations.

r001.rationale: It mentions measuring experimental progress, but does not raise how to measure intelligence to assess progress toward AGI.

r002.rationale: It does not present Shane Legg’s conception of AGI as a system capable of learning to complete any task.

r003.rationale: It describes games as a controlled setting for developing and testing capabilities associated with general intelligence.
